title: Eels Alive!
summary: Josh and Chuck (with iHeart Intro speaker) explore eels: what defines an eel (order Anguilliformes, about 800 species), how eels swim, moray eels and their jaws and teeth, garden eels, gulper eels, the eel as food in Japan and medieval Europe and the Americas, eels used as currency, and the long-standing mystery of eel reproduction solved through work by Carlo Mondini, Freud, Eugène Bataillon, Giovanni Battista Grassi, Johannes Schmidt, and the Sargasso Sea spawning discovery by Rosalind Wright's team. They close with eel conservation (IUCN Red List status, population declines, dams, aquaculture relying on wild glass eels, Maine elvers fishery) and a listener mail about homemade baking soda and coconut oil deodorant.

segments.title: Opening banter and David Byrne inspiration
segments.summary: Hosts chat about recent books and films, and credit David Byrne's book and videos as the inspiration for the episode on eels.

segments.title: What defines an eel
segments.summary: Eels are members of the order Anguilliformes, with about 20 families, 111 genera and over 800 species, ranging from about four inches to twelve feet. Electric eels are not true eels but knifefish.

segments.title: Eel anatomy, swimming and slime
segments.summary: Eels lack pelvic fins and swim in a wave-like motion, can swim backward by reversing the wave, and have slime coating that aids swimming and regulates water in the body. Eels also undergo metamorphosis.

segments.title: Magnetic navigation and eel migration
segments.summary: Eels migrate long distances to spawning areas and are thought to use magnetite in their bodies to navigate, though this is not proven.

segments.title: Moray eels and garden eels
segments.summary: Moray eels, about 200 species making up roughly a quarter of eels, hide in coral holes and have a second set of pharyngeal jaws. They show teeth because they lack opercula and pump water through their mouths. Their bites are painful due to mucus-related and toxin effects. Garden eels live in colonies in sand and feed on plankton.

segments.title: Conger eel and largest eels
segments.summary: The European conger is deep-water and is the heaviest eel; the largest recorded weighed 242 pounds.

segments.title: Josh Clark Calculates website plug
segments.summary: Brandon Reid's website Josh Clark Calculates lets users compare measurements using everyday objects.

segments.title: Gulper eels and deep-sea species
segments.summary: Gulper eels, also called pelican eels, live five to ten thousand feet deep and have a huge jaw that can unhinge and work as a scoop.

segments.title: Eels as food in Japan and North America
segments.summary: Freshwater eels are nutritious and were a major food source; unagi is popular in Japan and was one of the Edo period's big four foods. Indigenous peoples in northeastern North America also ate eels, preserved by smoking and salting.

segments.title: Eels in medieval Europe and currency
segments.summary: Europeans trapped eels in willow traps; dried eels were used as currency and to pay rent in England, and were popular during fasting seasons. Mention of a To Kill a Mockingbird scene.

segments.title: Early eel reproduction theories and Mondini and Freud
segments.summary: Ancient people had theories about eel reproduction since no one saw eggs. In 1777 Carlo Mondini located eel ovaries; Sigmund Freud later searched for and identified eel testes in 1876.

segments.title: Life cycle stages and leptocephalus larvae
segments.summary: Eel life stages include glass eel, elver, yellow eel and silver eel. Leptocephalus willow-leaf larvae were misidentified as a separate fish until a French researcher raised one through metamorphosis.

segments.title: Giovanni Battista Grassi and Schmidt's Sargasso search
segments.summary: An Italian zoologist observed metamorphosis in the wild. Johannes Schmidt, funded by the Carlsberg Foundation, traced larvae across the Atlantic and in 1912 proposed the Sargasso Sea as the breeding ground.

segments.title: Sargasso Sea and eel spawning confirmed
segments.summary: The Sargasso Sea is a calm, warm, saline gyre in the Atlantic. A European team led by Rosalind Wright confirmed in 2018 that eels spawn there. Japanese eels spawn near the Mariana Ridge; African longfin eels in the Indian Ocean. Eels migrate from European rivers across the Atlantic, similar to salmon, with the term catadromous.

segments.title: Eel conservation and the fishery
segments.summary: The IUCN lists European eels as critically endangered and American, Japanese and New Zealand longfin eels as endangered. Eel populations fell over 90 percent since the 1970s due to dams, turbines, overfishing, wetland loss and pollution. Eels are farmed by capturing wild glass eels. Maine is the only state with a glass eel fishery, with about 425 licensed elvermen shipping to Hong Kong.

segments.title: Wrap-up and eel vocabulary
segments.summary: Hosts joke about the term antepenultimate and say they will stop eating American and European eels.

segments.title: Listener mail on baking soda deodorant
segments.summary: Listener Alex follows up on a baking soda and coconut oil deodorant recipe, suggesting cornstarch as a neutral diluent to reduce skin irritation and noting coconut oil stains clothing.
